content: In Kenya, Lesotho, Mozambique, Rwanda, and Zimbabwe, structured interviews were conducted with healthcare workers providing infant testing services, as well as semi-structured interviews with national and regional laboratory managers or early infant diagnosis program managers, both before and after the implementation of point-of-care (POC) infant testing. Healthcare workers found POC infant testing to be user-friendly, with 74% describing it as very simple to perform. Additionally, 93% expressed high satisfaction with the rapid turnaround time and the ability to initiate treatment for HIV-positive infants more quickly. All healthcare workers recommended expanding POC infant testing in their countries, and 87% desired a POC testing device in their healthcare facilities. Laboratory managers also supported scaling up POC testing but emphasized the importance of reliable infrastructure to support these platforms. An online survey of 51 healthcare workers and 53 program managers was conducted to assess the acceptability and feasibility of implementing POC infant testing. Among healthcare workers, 88% felt comfortable performing the test, delivering results, counseling, and initiating same-day treatment. Most healthcare workers (77%) believed POC testing would be acceptable, and 65% preferred it if available. Additionally, 88% thought mothers would accept same-day infant testing and, in some cases, positive diagnoses. However, 45% of healthcare workers anticipated an increased workload in clinics but believed sufficient human resources were available to implement the program. Among the 53 program managers surveyed, 72% reported that their countries already had policies for POC infant testing, but 85% noted that most infant tests were still conducted using standard laboratory-based methods. A majority (55%) considered POC infant testing preferable and feasible, and more than half (55%) did not believe it would increase the workload in laboratories or clinics. A systematic review of diagnostic accuracy for POC technologies revealed high performance, with sensitivity exceeding 98% and specificity over 99%. Several POC technologies are available, with two already prequalified by the World Health Organization (WHO). Devices such as the Abbott m-PIMA™ and Cepheid GeneXpert® are widely used for tuberculosis (TB) and infant HIV diagnosis. These devices use whole blood and do not require additional equipment or expertise. The Abbott m-PIMA™ can process 6–8 tests per day, while the GeneXpert® can perform 6–8 tests per module daily. Across 140 high-burden developing countries, over 11,600 GeneXpert® devices (comprising 52,000 modules) have been delivered, with capacity available for expanding TB and HIV infant testing. Infant diagnosis should remain a priority when technologies are shared across programs. In most high HIV-burden countries, a small proportion of healthcare facilities serve the majority of HIV-exposed infants. For example, in Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, and Zambia, 80% of HIV-exposed infants attended only 32%, 33%, 12%, and 10% of healthcare facilities, respectively. This suggests that targeted placement of POC technologies could significantly impact HIV-exposed infants. Ethical and equity considerations emphasized the fair distribution of benefits and burdens, ensuring that infants are not disadvantaged compared to others in their communities. The introduction of POC testing should not preclude the provision of other essential health resources. The WHO Guideline Development Group strongly recommended POC nucleic acid testing (NAT) for diagnosing HIV in infants and children under 18 months, citing numerous benefits, including faster testing and result delivery, improved retention in the testing-to-treatment cascade, fewer clinic visits, increased equity with adult HIV testing, and faster antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, which may reduce mortality. No significant harms were identified, though higher costs and the need for technical support were noted. Implementation considerations highlighted the need for integrated diagnostic networks combining laboratory-based and POC technologies. Optimal placement of POC devices should align with overall health system needs, including other disease programs. Adequate human resources, training, and quality assurance are essential for successful implementation. Clear communication and collaboration with community groups are critical to building trust and ensuring utilization. Research gaps include the need for further studies on quality assurance approaches for sustainable POC testing delivery. Investigating dual-use POC tests for infants, children, and adults could streamline supply chains and improve diagnostic efficiency. Device-free tests resembling traditional rapid diagnostic tests are also being developed, which could decentralize testing further and reduce costs. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HIV serology can reliably detect HIV antibodies in children but cannot distinguish maternal antibodies from those produced by the child. In contrast, for children over 18 months, RDTs can definitively diagnose HIV infection as maternal antibodies are no longer present. However, antibody testing should not be used to confirm or rule out infection in children already receiving ART, as they may falsely test HIV-negative. The WHO recommends RDTs with a minimum sensitivity of 99% and specificity of 98%, particularly in resource-limited settings. To improve diagnostic accuracy, the WHO recommends introducing an indeterminate range for nucleic acid-based early infant diagnosis assays. This range would identify specimens requiring repeat testing, reducing false-positive results and unnecessary lifelong treatment. Clear communication with caregivers about the meaning of indeterminate results is essential to avoid confusion. In summary, POC testing for HIV in infants offers significant benefits, including faster diagnosis, improved treatment initiation, and increased equity. However, careful implementation, adequate training, and quality assurance are critical to its success. Further research and innovation in diagnostic technologies will enhance the sustainability and effectiveness of these programs.
